items.title: 60499_Garvin Bushell oral history interview
items.q: this gangster -- Harry Lyons said, "You better not take that band out of here."

ctx.x: And we didn't have to rehearse a tune. We'd say, 'Well, let's play this tune.' Everybody knew it. I tell my boys -- my students -- you never learn a melody unless you learn the harmony at the same time, because if you don't know the harmony, you don't know the music. You don't know it. So, everybody was familiar with the harmony of everything we played. And it was just fantastic how we could play four-part -- not three-part -- four-part harmony. Bingie Madison was a very qualified arranger. He was a master of…

salary, but I averaged -- and we worked seven nights a week, too, you see, and you had $130, $140, $150.00 a week. You could figure on that. And that was right during the depression. The depression started in '30, you know, because the crash was in '29, and that was in '30 when things were rough. Musicians were hungry. But we had that job -- so, something happened. Snowden- told him we wanted a raise. Said he wouldn't give it to us. So, we said, "Well, we quit." Snowden gave him his notice. So, it's time to quit,…

we're sitting on the job -- I was his straw boss when we were playing at Small's Paradise. A guy came in, "Who's got the keys to that blue Chrysler out there?" "Who wants to know?" "Finance." Snowden said, "You got them, Garvin?" "No, I forgot them." He looked at me -- he knew I had the keys. Snowden says, "No, he don't have the keys." He said, "Well, I'm going to haul it, I'm going to take it away." And sure enough, they took our Chrysler away from us, right while we were on the job. We were making money -- the…
